news.title: Anthropic commits 5% of its shares to a new Public Benefit Fund
news.summary: Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic will put 5% of its shares into a new public-benefit entity, with more possible as its valuation grows. The fund will back nonprofit grants and labor-market work and cannot be used for lobbying.

news.title: Anthropic acquires confidential-AI startup Opaque Systems
news.summary: Anthropic struck a licensing and acquihire deal that brings over Opaque's CEO, CTO and several engineers, adding confidential-computing and agent-governance tools to its enterprise lineup.

news.title: Anthropic's private benefit trust faces scrutiny ahead of its IPO
news.summary: The WSJ examines the five-member Long-Term Benefit Trust, which holds no equity but has picked four of seven board directors, and whose agreement remains unpublished ahead of a planned November listing.

news.title: Sam Altman confirms OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, with a 2027 demo planned
news.summary: Altman said OpenAI is developing a humanoid robot it expects to show in 2027; the company is hiring for dozens of robotics roles.

news.title: Microsoft pulls out of Nscale's planned Essex AI data center
news.summary: Microsoft withdrew as the anchor customer of a site billed as one of the UK's largest AI computing projects; Nscale says it still plans to build.

news.title: DeepSeek releases V4.1-Flash-1017 with open weights and a web search API
news.summary: DeepSeek published an MIT-licensed update to its fast sparse mixture-of-experts model, tuned for agent and coding work, and opened Search and Fetch APIs for live web retrieval.

news.title: Reflection AI opens Beam, a 501B-parameter model that aims to use fewer tokens
news.summary: Reflection released Beam under Apache 2.0, a mixture-of-experts model with 23B active parameters for coding and agents, pitched as matching rivals while generating far fewer tokens.

news.title: Claude helps trace the mysterious seeds of NIST's elliptic curves
news.summary: Anthropic researchers say Claude found, in under half an hour, that several long-unexplained NIST curve seeds likely came from an old C random-number generator seeded with timestamps, weakening backdoor theories.

news.title: Nvidia's Vera team says agentic AI is pushing CPUs back toward single-thread speed
news.summary: Nvidia engineers argue agent workloads need fast CPU-GPU coordination, and claim the monolithic Vera CPU delivers 1.5x the performance of Grace.

news.title: Rivian is building its own AI models and a 5nm autonomy chip
news.summary: Rivian is developing in-vehicle AI models and an autonomous driving stack in-house, and co-designing a 5nm chip with Arm and TSMC.

news.title: Meta blames a Claude-linked scraper for a mistaken Instagram suspension
news.summary: Meta said high-speed access by a Claude-linked tool tripped bot detection and briefly suspended No Kings Coalition accounts, without naming the tool's operator.

news.title: Illinois governor creates a state AI Cabinet
news.summary: An executive order from JB Pritzker sets up an AI Cabinet to shape Illinois AI policy through 2027, including risks to residents and critical infrastructure.

papers.title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
papers.tldr: Robots searching homes for objects often reach the goal but fail to stop; a separate 'spotter' model that says what's in view and how far fixes much of this.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
StopWatch helps a robot that is hunting for an object, like "find a chair", notice when that object is already in front of it, so it actually stops in the right place.

## Background you need
In object-goal navigation, a robot is dropped into a home it has never seen and told to find an object category. It must explore, find an example of that object, and stop close to it. Many recent systems start from a vision-language model (an AI that reads both images and text) and fine-tune it to output movement commands. This direct approach is called an end-to-end policy (one model that maps camera images straight to actions).

## The problem
These robots often get very close to the goal and then fail anyway. On one standard test set, an end-to-end policy came within a quarter of a metre of the goal in about 76% of trials. Yet it succeeded in only about 52%. The robot explores well but does not realise it has arrived.

The authors call this a goal grounding problem: linking the word "chair" to a specific thing in the camera view, and judging how far away it is. Training by copying expert demonstrations gives little signal about when to stop. The gap is worst for object types the robot never saw in training.

## The idea
Split the job between a spotter and a driver. Think of a rally car with a co-driver who reads the map aloud: "the turn is visible, 50 metres ahead." The driver no longer has to read the map while steering. StopWatch adds a "spotter" model that writes a short note about what is in view, and a "driver" model that reads that note before choosing a move.

## How it works
1. **Write grounding notes for training.** For every training frame, the authors generate a short text from the 3D scene labels. It lists the objects in view, whether the goal is visible, and a rough distance band to it.
2. **Train the spotter.** A perception model, fine-tuned from a 4-billion-parameter vision-language model, learns to write that note from the last few camera frames plus the goal word.
3. **Train the driver.** A smaller 2-billion-parameter model learns to pick the next action from the camera images and the note. During training it gets perfect, label-derived notes.
4. **Combine at test time.** The driver now reads the spotter's predicted note instead of the perfect one. The two models are trained separately.
5. **Clean the benchmarks.** The authors found labelling mistakes in the test scenes. They merged 2,408 raw object labels into 540 classes and dropped broken episodes, about 23% of one test set.

## Results
StopWatch had the best success rate on all six benchmarks, across three collections of simulated homes. On the cleaned version of the hardest common test, with unseen object types, it succeeded 69.6% of the time. The strongest earlier method, LightNav-0, reached 60.8%. That is roughly nine more successful searches out of every hundred.

On one collection of scenes the gap was larger: 56.4% versus 36.3% for the next best method, VLFM. When the driver was given perfect notes instead of predicted ones, success jumped to 91.6%. That suggests the driver is nearly solved and most remaining errors come from the spotter's perception.

## Why it matters
Home robots, warehouse robots and assistive devices all need to find things and stop at the right spot. This work shows a cheap fix: make "is the goal here, and how far?" an explicit, checkable step. It also points researchers to the real bottleneck, which is perception rather than movement. The cleaned benchmarks should make future comparisons fairer.

## Caveats
Everything was tested in simulation, in static indoor scenes. Real-robot transfer is expected but not shown. Training the spotter needs 3D scenes with detailed object and geometry labels, which limits how much data can be used. The authors list learning from unlabelled real videos as future work. Running two models instead of one may also add some compute cost.

## Key terms
- **Object-goal navigation:** finding and stopping near an object of a named type in an unfamiliar place.
- **Vision-language model:** an AI model that takes in both pictures and text.
- **End-to-end policy:** a single model that turns sensor input directly into actions.
- **Goal grounding:** connecting a word like "chair" to the actual object in view and its distance.
- **Behavior cloning:** training a robot by having it copy recorded expert actions.

papers.title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: Agents on long tasks do better and read up to half as much text when they keep compact, evidence-checked progress records instead of full interaction logs.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
CarryOn is a way for AI agents doing long jobs to keep a tidy, up-to-date record of the progress they have made, instead of dragging around a huge transcript of everything they did.

## Background you need
An AI agent is a language model that takes actions, such as clicking around a computer or searching the web, to finish a task. Everything it can "see" at once is its context window (the text the model reads before each step). On long tasks this window fills up. Systems then "fold" the context, meaning they compress or drop older parts to make room.

## The problem
Most agents store their past as a growing log of interactions: every command, every page, every result. That log is long, repetitive and expensive, because the model pays for every token (word piece) it reads at each step. When the log is folded, useful progress can be lost or summarised wrongly. On long computer-use and web-research tasks, this means more cost and more failures.

## The idea
Pack light. A traveller on a long trip does not carry every receipt. They carry the passport, the tickets and a short list of what is booked. CarryOn applies this to agents. It organises memory around reusable pieces of task progress, which the authors call continuation carriers, rather than around the history that produced them. The history is the receipts. The carriers are the passport and tickets.

## How it works
1. **Keep progress as records.** As the agent works, CarryOn stores the useful outcomes, such as facts found or sub-steps completed, as separate records ("carriers").
2. **Build each view fresh.** Before each step, the model sees a view built from three parts: the carriers, extra execution context that complements them, and only the most recent interactions.
3. **Tie records to evidence.** Each record is bound to the evidence that supports it, such as a page or a check of the environment's state.
4. **Revise only what changed.** When the context is folded, CarryOn does not rewrite everything. It re-checks and updates only the records affected by new evidence, so the rest stay valid.

## Results
The authors tested CarryOn on two long-horizon benchmarks. OSWorld 2.0 has agents operate a real computer desktop. BrowseComp-Plus has agents dig through the web for hard-to-find answers.

They report task performance gains of 5.8% on OSWorld 2.0 and 7.0% on BrowseComp-Plus. At the same time, token use dropped by 51.9% and 22.9%. In practice, on the desktop tasks the agent read about half as much text while doing better. Less text read means lower bills and faster steps.

## Why it matters
Long agent tasks, like filling out forms across several apps or doing a research report, are where today's agents struggle and cost the most. A memory design that both cuts tokens and raises success could make such agents cheaper to run. The idea is also model-agnostic: it changes what the model reads, not the model itself. That means it could slot into existing agent products.

## Caveats
This summary is based on the paper's abstract and listing, as the full text was not readable at the time of writing. So the exact baselines and models behind the gains are not described here. Results come from two benchmarks only. Building and checking records against evidence adds engineering complexity, and how well it handles messy, ambiguous evidence is an open question. Reported percentages should be read against the specific baselines in the paper.

## Key terms
- **AI agent:** a language model that takes actions in software to complete a task.
- **Context window:** the text the model can read at once before deciding its next step.
- **Context folding:** compressing or dropping old parts of the context to make room.
- **Token:** a small chunk of text; models are billed and slowed by how many they read.
- **Continuation carrier:** CarryOn's term for a stored record of reusable task progress.

papers.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
papers.tldr: A draft model that ignores long conversation history and reuses the big model's internal summary keeps speculative decoding fast on agent workloads.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
DLite makes AI agents reply faster by using a tiny "guessing" model that ignores the long conversation history and only looks at what is happening right now.

## Background you need
Large language models write one token (a small chunk of text) at a time, which is slow. Speculative decoding speeds this up. A small draft model quickly guesses several next tokens, and the big target model checks them all in one go. Acceptance length is how many guessed tokens are accepted per check on average; higher means faster. The KV cache is the model's short-term memory of text it has already read.

## The problem
Agent workloads break this trick. Agents have long, ever-changing contexts and many back-and-forth turns with tools. The authors found that existing draft models can lose up to 80% of their acceptance length in these settings. So most of the speedup disappears.

Draft models also keep their own copy of the history in a KV cache. For long agent sessions, managing that cache adds real system overhead. Both problems come from the same source: the growing history.

## The idea
Stop making the guesser read the whole history. Think of a court stenographer's assistant who predicts the next few words. They do not need to re-read the whole trial. They only need the speaker's current sentence and the judge's notes. DLite's draft model drops the history and borrows a compact summary from the big model instead.

## How it works
1. **Borrow the big model's understanding.** The target model already produces hidden states (its internal numerical summary of the context). DLite reuses these as the draft model's view of the past.
2. **Predict locally.** The draft model only looks at a small local window. This turns a hard long-sequence problem into a simpler local one, and removes the draft model's own history cache.
3. **Restore word order cheaply.** Guessing a block of tokens independently can produce words that do not fit together. A light "sequential head" re-adds the dependency of each guessed token on the previous ones inside the block.
4. **Train in two stages.** Because this design mixes different parts, the authors use a two-stage training plan to fit them together.

## Results
Across general chat, long-context and agent benchmarks, DLite reached acceptance lengths of about 2 to 6 tokens per check. In plain terms, each expensive check of the big model accepts between two and six words instead of one.

Compared with DSpark, which the authors describe as the previous state of the art, DLite improved by up to 70%. The authors also say dropping history avoids the cache overhead that earlier draft models carry. The exact wall-clock speedups per model are reported in the paper.

## Why it matters
Agents are becoming a major way people use AI, for coding, browsing and office tasks. They are also slow and costly, because each step waits for the model to write. A draft model that keeps working well on long, messy agent sessions could cut waiting time and serving cost. Removing the draft model's cache also frees memory on the GPU for more users.

## Caveats
This summary is based on the paper's abstract and Hugging Face page, as the full text was not readable at the time of writing. The "up to 70%" is a best case; typical gains may be smaller. Dropping history could hurt on tasks where the next words depend on something said long ago, if the borrowed hidden states miss it. Results depend on the specific target models tested, and the two-stage training adds setup cost.

## Key terms
- **Speculative decoding:** a small model guesses tokens and a big model verifies them in bulk.
- **Draft model:** the small, fast guessing model.
- **Acceptance length:** average number of guessed tokens accepted per verification.
- **KV cache:** stored memory of already-read text, kept to avoid recomputing it.
- **Hidden states:** a model's internal numerical summary of what it has read.

papers.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Letting the draft model read a hybrid model's running memory makes speculative decoding about 3x faster than normal generation.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
ReaDy speeds up a newer kind of language model by letting its fast "guessing" helper peek at the big model's running memory, so its guesses are right more often.

## Background you need
Speculative decoding speeds up text generation. A small draft model guesses several next tokens (text chunks), and the big target model verifies them in one pass. Standard attention re-reads all past text each step, which gets costly. Linear attention models instead keep a fixed-size recurrent state (a running summary updated as each token arrives). Hybrid linear attention models mix both kinds of layers to get speed with good quality.

## The problem
Draft models for these hybrid models usually see only limited information about the conversation so far. That makes their guesses less accurate, and every wrong guess wastes work. Meanwhile, the big model already holds a rich running summary in its recurrent states. Existing drafters do not use it. As hybrid models spread, serving them fast becomes a practical cost issue for anyone running them.

## The idea
Let the guesser read the big model's notebook. Imagine a sous-chef guessing the next steps of a recipe. They will guess much better if they can glance at the head chef's running notes than if they only see the last dish. ReaDy gives each guessed position a cheap way to look up extra context from the target model's recurrent states.

## How it works
1. **Start from a strong drafter.** ReaDy builds on DSpark, an existing drafting design with a parallel backbone and a sequential prediction head that keeps guessed tokens consistent with each other.
2. **Add a state reader.** A lightweight module lets every draft position pull extra context from the target model's recurrent states.
3. **Keep it cheap.** The reader uses low-rank reads (compact, small-matrix lookups) so it adds little compute.
4. **Blend it in gently.** The retrieved context is added through residual updates, meaning it is added on top of what the drafter already computes rather than replacing it.
5. **Train in two stages.** A two-stage adaptation strategy fits the new reader to the existing drafter.

## Results
The authors tested on seven benchmarks covering math, code generation and dialogue. Using the Qwen3.8-27B hybrid model on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, ReaDy decoded on average 3.16 times faster than normal one-token-at-a-time generation. In practice, a reply that took about 6 seconds would take roughly 2.

ReaDy also beat DSpark on every one of the seven benchmarks. The size of each gain is reported in the paper.

## Why it matters
Hybrid linear attention models are attractive because their memory use grows slowly with long inputs. But they need their own serving tricks, since tools built for standard models do not fit perfectly. ReaDy shows that the recurrent state, which these models keep anyway, is a free and useful signal for drafting. Companies serving such models could get faster, cheaper replies with a small add-on.

## Caveats
This summary is based on the paper's abstract, as the full text was not readable at the time of writing. The main speed number comes from one model on one GPU type. Gains on other hybrid models, longer agent sessions or batched serving with many users are not covered here. The method applies only to models that have recurrent states, not to standard attention-only models.

## Key terms
- **Speculative decoding:** a fast model guesses tokens and a big model checks them in bulk.
- **Linear attention:** an attention style that keeps a fixed-size running summary instead of re-reading everything.
- **Recurrent state:** that running summary, updated with each new token.
- **Hybrid model:** a model mixing standard attention layers with linear attention layers.
- **Low-rank read:** a compact, cheap lookup using small matrices.

papers.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
papers.tldr: A new way of wiring the layers of a large language model lets each layer look back at earlier layers through several different views, reaching the same training loss with about 1.58x less compute for under 1% extra cost.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
MSAR changes how the layers of a large language model hand information to each other: each layer looks back at all earlier layers through four different views, so training reaches the same quality with noticeably less compute.

## Background you need
A language model is a tall stack of layers. Between them sits a residual connection (the standard wiring that adds each layer's output onto one running total flowing upward). An earlier method, Attention Residuals (AttnRes), replaced that plain sum with depth attention: each layer learns how much to pull from each earlier layer. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model is one where each word only uses a few of many sub-networks, so the model can be huge but cheap per word.

## The problem
With a plain running sum, features from early layers get diluted as the network grows deeper. AttnRes helped, but each layer still makes only one retrieval choice, like attention with a single head. Earlier attempts to add more heads failed. Splitting the hidden vector into channel groups hurt quality. Hyper-Connection-style designs, which keep several parallel copies of the residual stream, produced heads that looked almost identical after normalization.

## The idea
Picture a writer who consults an archive of their past notes. AttnRes is one assistant fetching notes with one search query. MSAR hires four assistants. Each reads the archive through a different-sized window: one sees each word alone, the others also see the last 4, 8 or 12 words around it. An editor blends their findings. The variety comes from different views of the same notes, not from cutting the notes into pieces.

## How it works
1. **Make several views.** For every earlier layer's output, MSAR builds four versions: the original plus three passed through cheap causal convolutions (small filters that mix in only the preceding words) with window sizes 4, 8 and 12.
2. **Attend separately.** Each view has its own learned query and its own weighting over all earlier layers. So each head can favor different past layers.
3. **Blend into one.** A tiny mixer computes one weight per view from the input and sums the four results into a single input for the next layer. Only one stream is ever stored, which avoids the memory and communication cost of multi-stream designs.
4. **Group layers into blocks.** Layers are bundled into blocks that each keep a single summary. The four views are created on the fly only when needed, using fused GPU kernels so temporary data never goes back to memory.

## Results
The authors trained MoE models with 18 billion and 28 billion total parameters and tested them on 12 benchmarks covering general knowledge, code, math and Chinese understanding.
- At 18B, final training loss was 1.750 for MSAR, versus 1.769 for AttnRes, 1.776 for manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and 1.799 for standard residuals.
- Average downstream score at 18B: 45.7 for MSAR against 41.8, 41.7 and 37.5 for the same baselines.
- At 28B: 52.4 against 49.4, 47.4 and 44.6.
- In scaling experiments, MSAR matched the standard model's loss with 1.58x less compute (AttnRes: 1.35x, mHC: 1.30x). Put simply, a run needing 158 GPU-days reaches the same loss in about 100.
- The extra cost at 28B was about 0.5% more training compute and 0.3% more active parameters.

## Why it matters
Residual wiring sits inside every modern language model. A change that costs under 1% extra but saves roughly a third of training compute is attractive to any lab doing large pretraining runs. Because MSAR stores only one stream, it fits pipeline-parallel training (splitting layers across GPUs) without extra communication.

## Caveats
- The text reports compute counts, not measured wall-clock speed. Writing and blending the four retrieved views still adds memory traffic.
- Experiments come from one group and top out at 28B parameters. Training token budgets were not stated in the parts I could read.
- Four views with windows 4, 8 and 12 are a design choice; whether other settings work better at larger scales is open.

## Key terms
- **Residual connection**: wiring that adds each layer's output onto a running total passed upward.
- **Depth attention**: letting a layer choose, with learned weights, which earlier layers to read from.
- **Causal convolution**: a small sliding filter that mixes each word with only the words before it.
- **Mixture-of-experts (MoE)**: a model where each word uses only a few of many specialist sub-networks.
- **Iso-loss compute speedup**: how much less compute a method needs to reach the same training loss.

papers.title: Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
papers.tldr: Instead of always sending each word to exactly 8 experts during training, this method randomly picks between about 6 and 10, which trains better mixture-of-experts models at the same average cost and with no change at inference.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The paper trains mixture-of-experts language models by letting the number of experts each word uses wobble randomly around its usual value, which gives better models at the same average cost.

## Background you need
A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model contains many small specialist sub-networks called experts. For each word, a router (a small scoring network) rates all experts and sends the word to the top k of them, for example the top 8. Only those experts run, which keeps the model cheap. During training, only the chosen experts get a gradient (the learning signal that tells them how to improve).

## The problem
A fixed k creates a hard cliff. Suppose expert number 8 scores 0.101 and expert number 9 scores 0.100. The first gets full training feedback; the second gets none, even though the router barely prefers one over the other. The authors argue that this makes learning near the cutoff fragile, because tiny score wobbles decide who learns. Earlier fixes that vary k tend to change the compute budget at deployment, alter the model's structure, or lose quality when compute is tight.

## The idea
Think of a school team that always picks exactly 8 players for every match. Player 9 never gets game time, so the coach never learns how good they are. If the coach instead fields 6 to 10 players depending on the day, averaging 8, the players near the cutoff all get some real experience. Total playing time stays the same, but the selection becomes better informed.

## How it works
1. **Draw a budget.** For every word and every layer during training, the method samples how many experts to use from a bell-shaped distribution centered on 8. The main setting allows 6 to 10.
2. **Route as usual.** The word goes to that many top-ranked experts. Experts beyond that number are masked out.
3. **Balance the load.** The usual load-balancing penalty (which stops a few experts from getting all the work) is computed from the experts actually used.
4. **Keep cost flat.** Because the draw is symmetric around 8, the average number of experts stays exactly 8. Expected training compute matches standard top-8.
5. **Deploy unchanged.** At inference the model goes back to plain top-8 routing. Nothing about the architecture changes.

## Results
The authors fine-tuned two existing MoE models and also trained one from scratch.
- **OLMoE-1B-7B, fine-tuned on instructions:** average score over nine tasks rose from 30.57 with fixed top-8 to 31.41 with the 6-to-10 schedule (+0.84).
- **Qwen3-30B-A3B, fine-tuned:** the average rose from 56.42 to 58.44 (+2.02). An elastic schedule won on eight of nine tasks.
- **Pretraining from scratch:** a model with 1.42 billion total parameters, 128 experts per layer, trained on 26.25 billion words of educational web text. The average downstream score rose from 41.3 to 42.9. On LAMBADA, a next-word test, perplexity (a measure of how surprised the model is; lower is better) fell from 54.2 to 42.7.
- Wider ranges were not always better: 5-to-11 scored below 6-to-10 in every setting. So a moderate wobble works best.
- Routing analysis showed the trained routers changed most in a middle block of layers (layers 3 to 7 of 16 in OLMoE).

## Why it matters
The change is a few lines in the training loop. It adds no parameters and leaves inference cost and model shape untouched. So teams fine-tuning open MoE models, or pretraining new ones, could adopt it with almost no engineering risk. It also offers a cleaner way to think about routing: as how often each expert gets exposed to learning, not just which expert wins.

## Caveats
- Only two fine-tuning backbones and one small pretraining scale were tested.
- The text does not report multiple random seeds, so it is hard to judge whether gains under one point are reliable.
- Measured wall-clock time and memory are in an appendix I could not read; variable expert counts can make GPU work less even across devices.
- The 'fragile cliff' story is supported by indirect diagnostics, not a direct experiment.

## Key terms
- **Mixture-of-experts (MoE)**: a model that sends each word to a few of many specialist sub-networks.
- **Router**: the small network that scores experts and picks which ones run.
- **Top-k routing**: always choosing the k highest-scoring experts.
- **Gradient**: the learning signal that tells a part of the model how to change.
- **Perplexity**: how surprised a model is by real text; lower means better predictions.

papers.title: RESOLVE: Language-Agnostic Validation of GPU Kernels Through Testing, Reduction, and Proof
papers.tldr: RESOLVE checks whether a fast GPU kernel, including one written by an AI agent, really computes the same thing as a trusted reference, by combining race-hunting tests, simplification and formal proof.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
RESOLVE is a tool chain that checks whether an optimized GPU program truly matches a trusted reference, first by hunting for timing bugs and then by mathematically proving the two compute the same function.

## Background you need
A kernel is a small program that runs on a GPU, with thousands of threads working at once. AI agents now write and tune kernels faster than people can review them. The usual check is to run both the new kernel and a simple reference on random inputs and see if the outputs match within a tolerance (an allowed rounding gap). A race condition is a bug where the result depends on which thread happens to finish first.

## The problem
Random testing misses races that show up only under unlucky timing. Tolerances cut both ways: loose ones hide real bugs, and tight ones reject correct kernels that merely add numbers in a different order. Formal verification (machine-checked mathematical proof) would cover every input. But existing GPU verifiers do not model modern features such as tensor cores (special matrix units), warp-level shortcuts or asynchronous memory copies. As AI-written kernels spread into production, this gap matters.

## The idea
Think of inspecting a busy restaurant kitchen. First you deliberately shake up the timing, delaying cooks at random, to see if any dish changes. Next you write down a slow, one-cook version of each recipe that makes the exact same dish. Finally you prove, on paper, that both one-cook recipes produce the same meal. Splitting 'does timing matter?' from 'is the math right?' makes each question manageable.

## How it works
1. **Shake the timing.** RESOLVE instruments the compiled machine code with a tool called NVBit. It finds memory accesses that could conflict and inserts delays only there. If any output differs from normal runs, it reports nondeterminism. Because it works on machine code, it handles CUDA, Triton, Gluon and CUTLASS alike.
2. **Simplify.** An AI agent rewrites both the candidate and the reference into reduced-concurrency versions with far less parallelism. These must match the originals bit for bit on every test, with zero tolerance.
3. **Prove.** A verifier called Kuiper, built on the F* proof language, checks both simplified kernels against one mathematical specification written from the reference. It reasons over real numbers, so two kernels that round differently can still be proven equivalent.

## Results
Tests ran on NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
- On 100 basic KernelBench problems paired with AI-optimized candidates, 41 had no possible conflicts. Two candidates were empty and did nothing, yet both passed KernelBench's usual tolerance tests.
- Of 14 kernels taken through the full chain, 11 were simplified and formally proven correct. Two hit features the prover lacks. One used a Taylor-series approximation of a math function that is close but not exactly equivalent, and was rightly rejected.
- A full check took a median of about 143 minutes, mostly writing the specification and proof (about 112 minutes).
- In a test with 143 deliberately injected bugs, the timing tester caught 92 (about 64%). Of the 51 misses, 28 were harmless races that never changed output and 20 were inside a single warp, beyond the tool's reach.
- It proved that fused MLP kernels (a common model block) written in Triton, Gluon and CUTLASS match the PyTorch reference.
- All three large 'mega-kernels' studied were nondeterministic. The team traced four root causes, including two clear bugs. Agent-written fixes changed speed by between -1.6% and +10.5%.

## Why it matters
As companies let AI agents write performance-critical GPU code, a passing test suite is not enough. RESOLVE shows that empty or subtly wrong kernels can slip through standard benchmarks. A method that gives real proofs, across several kernel languages, could become a safety gate for AI-generated code.

## Caveats
- Races inside a single warp and delays on asynchronous loads cannot be tested yet.
- A clean timing test is strong evidence, not proof, of race freedom.
- Kernels that differ by acceptable approximation are rejected, not accepted within an error budget.
- Specifications are checked by human review, and only 14 of 85 remaining KernelBench kernels went through full proof.
- The prover lacks some operations, and large multi-warp kernels could not be simplified.

## Key terms
- **Kernel**: a small program that runs in parallel on a GPU.
- **Race condition**: a bug where results depend on thread timing.
- **Formal verification**: a machine-checked proof that a program meets a specification for all inputs.
- **Tolerance**: the rounding gap allowed when comparing two outputs.
- **Warp**: a group of 32 GPU threads that execute in lockstep.

papers.title: Efficient FlashAttention on Blackwell via Fixed-Shift Softmax and Persistent Scheduling
papers.tldr: A Triton-based FlashAttention for NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs skips the usual running-maximum bookkeeping in softmax and schedules work more evenly, running 7.3% faster on average than FlashAttention-4.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors rewrote FlashAttention for NVIDIA's newest Blackwell GPUs, removing bookkeeping steps from the inner loop so attention runs about 7% faster on average than the current best version.

## Background you need
Attention is the step where a language model compares every word with every other word; it dominates cost on long inputs. FlashAttention computes it in small tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory, never writing the giant score table to slow main memory. Softmax (the step that turns scores into weights that sum to one) uses exponentials, which can overflow. So implementations subtract each row's maximum score first. The kernel here is written in TLX, a Triton-based language that exposes low-level control of the hardware.

## The problem
On Blackwell, the matrix units (tensor cores) got much faster, but the parts that compute exponentials and move data did not keep pace. Now the side work around the matrix math is the bottleneck. One example: FlashAttention tracks a running maximum per row. When a new tile has a bigger score, all earlier partial results must be rescaled before the next step can use them. That stalls the pipeline. Causal attention (where each word only sees earlier words) adds uneven work across tiles.

## The idea
Imagine converting prices from many shops into one currency. The usual approach waits to see the most expensive item and keeps re-adjusting earlier totals whenever a pricier one appears. The new approach picks a safe fixed reference price in advance. The final shares are mathematically identical, because softmax ignores any constant shift, and no re-adjusting is needed, as long as numbers stay in range.

## How it works
1. **Fixed shift.** For dense attention, a constant chosen at compile time replaces the running maximum. Earlier results never need rescaling.
2. **Cheaper exponentials.** Instead of the GPU's limited special-function unit, exponentials are built from ordinary arithmetic and bit tricks, two values at a time in 16-bit format.
3. **Safety net for causal attention.** The shift is anchored per row group, each group is checked, and failing tiles are redone with the standard method. Tiles that are fully masked are skipped entirely.
4. **Simpler backward pass.** The forward pass saves one reciprocal per row, so the training gradient pass can scale once up front instead of renormalizing every score.
5. **Better scheduling.** A persistent kernel (one that stays on the GPU and pulls work) pairs thread blocks into two-block clusters that share data and spread tiles evenly. Causal work is ordered to reuse cached data.

## Results
On an NVIDIA B200 GPU at 1,000 watts, across 24 test cases in 16-bit precision with inputs up to 32,768 tokens:
- Overall average throughput rose 7.3% over FlashAttention-4 (1,272 versus 1,185 trillion operations per second). A training step spending 10 seconds in attention would spend about 9.3.
- Dense forward +13.0%, dense backward +10.4%, causal backward +8.0%. Causal forward was 1.5% slower.
- Peak dense forward speed hit 1,787 trillion operations per second at 32,768 tokens, versus 1,583 for FlashAttention-4 in the authors' run.
- On TritonBench at 750 watts, estimated gains were 13.4% forward and 24.4% backward.
- All head-dimension-128 cases passed the accuracy check against a 32-bit reference.

## Why it matters
Attention is a large share of training and serving cost for long-context models. Gains of 10% or more on the backward pass translate directly into cheaper training runs on Blackwell clusters. The work also shows that, on new hardware, removing side work around the matrix math now matters as much as the math itself.

## Caveats
- Accuracy is lower than FlashAttention-4 in one gradient: relative error of 1.47e-2 versus 2.37e-3 at 32,768 tokens.
- The fast exponential trick can produce invalid values in some ranges, so deployments need range checks or a fallback.
- Each change was not measured separately, determinism was not tested, and each length used one random input.
- Code has not been publicly released.

## Key terms
- **FlashAttention**: a way of computing attention in small tiles kept in fast on-chip memory.
- **Softmax**: turns raw scores into positive weights that add up to one.
- **Causal attention**: each word may only look at earlier words.
- **Persistent kernel**: a GPU program that stays resident and fetches new work itself.
- **Tensor cores**: GPU units specialized for fast matrix multiplication.

papers.title: λ0: Scaling Open-World Egocentric Human Data for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: A 500-hour dataset of people filmed from their own viewpoint, converted into robot-ready training data, lets a humanoid foundation model learn to walk and handle objects together with little robot data.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The team recorded 500 hours of people doing everyday tasks while walking around, converted those recordings into "robot-shaped" training data, and used it to train λ0, a model that lets a humanoid robot move and handle objects at the same time.

## Background you need
A humanoid robot doing loco-manipulation must walk, crouch, lean and use its hands together, like carrying a box across a room. Robots usually learn this from demonstrations, where a human remote-controls the robot and the robot copies the recording. Egocentric data means video shot from the person's own head, so it shows what they saw. A vision-language-action model (VLA) is an AI that looks at camera images, reads an instruction, and outputs motor commands.

## The problem
Remote-controlling a whole humanoid is slow and needs a robot on site for every recording. That makes big datasets expensive. Recording humans is far cheaper, but existing first-person human datasets mostly capture hands, not walking or posture. Humans and robots also have different bodies. A motion that is natural for a person can make the robot's hand miss its target by many centimetres.

## The idea
Treat human recordings like a film that needs dubbing before a foreign audience can watch it. The team keeps the story (what the person did) but changes the "language". The camera view is made to match the robot's head camera. The human arms are replaced with drawn-in robot arms. Each motion is then retuned so the robot's controller actually lands the hand where the person's hand went.

## How it works
1. **Collect.** Volunteers wear a GoPro camera at the same height as the robot's head camera, plus a headset and body trackers. They get loose prompts like an activity name, not exact moves, and record in ordinary places. The result is HumanVerse: 32,993 episodes covering 827 task types.
2. **Fix the picture.** Software cuts out the human forearms and trackers, fills in the background, and draws the Unitree G1 robot's arms in their place.
3. **Fix the motion.** In three offline passes, the human pose is scaled to robot height, corrected so the hand targets stay reachable, and refined by replaying it on a simulated robot controller and nudging it until the hands land correctly.
4. **Train λ0 in three stages.** It is built on a 2-billion-parameter vision-language model (Qwen3.5-2B). It first learns hand motion from public first-person videos. Then it learns whole-body moves from the aligned HumanVerse data. Finally it is fine-tuned on a small amount of real robot data.

## Results
- The motion fix cut average hand-placement error from 17.03 cm to 3.83 cm. Orientation error fell from about 36° to about 11°. That is the difference between missing a cup handle and grabbing it.
- With human data only, and no robot recordings of the target tasks, the G1 averaged 62.2% task progress over seven tasks.
- Collecting a human demo took 33.30 person-seconds versus 140.85 for robot teleoperation. That is about 4.2× more demos per hour, though the authors note the two were measured differently.
- Whole-body human mid-training raised real-world task progress from 59.9% to 80.4%.
- λ0 reached 90.0% success in the SIMPLE simulation benchmark and 62.5% on four real tasks. It beat the strongest competing models, including π0.5 and StarVLA, by 3.9 and 22.5 percentage points.

## Why it matters
Humanoid companies are limited by how much whole-body training data they can gather. This work suggests ordinary people with a camera and trackers could gather much of it, with no robot present. It also shows that more human data keeps helping, which hints at a scalable path.

## Caveats
All tests use one robot, the Unitree G1, so other bodies are untested. Time-saving figures are rough estimates. Hand motion is reconstructed from video, which can be noisy. When alignment fails, the pipeline falls back to an uncorrected motion. Real-world tests used ten fixed starting setups per task, which may not reflect messy homes. 200 human demos still scored below 50 robot demos on two tasks (53.3% vs 60.0%).

## Key terms
- **Loco-manipulation**: moving the whole body and using the hands at the same time.
- **Egocentric video**: footage recorded from the person's own viewpoint.
- **Teleoperation**: a human steering the robot remotely to record examples.
- **Mid-training**: an in-between training stage, after general pre-training and before task-specific fine-tuning.
- **Zero-shot transfer**: working on a task without any robot examples of that task.

papers.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
papers.tldr: A robot hand trained in simulation spins two Baoding balls using only touch and joint sensing, with no cameras, and touch makes it about 7 times better than joint sensing alone.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
A robot hand learned to spin two Baoding balls around each other with its "eyes closed," using only touch sensors and a sense of its own finger positions, and kept it up for 112.5 full rotations.

## Background you need
Baoding balls are two metal balls you rotate around each other in one palm. It is hard because the balls bump into each other and into your fingers. Proprioception is the robot's sense of its own joints: where each finger is and how fast it moves. Reinforcement learning (RL) trains a controller by trial and error, rewarding good outcomes. Here, training happens in a physics simulator and the result is then copied to the real hand, which is called sim-to-real transfer.

## The problem
Most robot hands that juggle objects rely on cameras, motion-capture rigs, or perfect position data that only exists in simulation. Cameras get blocked by fingers, need lighting, and add cost. Earlier work showed blind Baoding rotation only in simulation, never on a real hand. Meanwhile, the gap between simulated and real hands often ruins policies that look perfect in software.

## The idea
Humans can roll the balls in a pocket without looking, because touch tells us where things are. The authors ask whether a robot can do the same. Think of it like a pianist playing by feel: the fingers' contact with the keys guides each move. The paper also asks how much touch actually adds compared to joint sense alone.

## How it works
1. **Hardware.** A Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite has 13 independently driven joints. It has 16 touch sensors: 12 pressure pads on the palm and finger segments, plus 4 fingertip sensors. Each sensor is reduced to a simple on/off "touching or not" signal.
2. **Faithful simulation.** The authors fixed how the simulated fingers bend. On the real hand the middle knuckle moves first and the tip follows later. They also placed simulated sensors exactly where the real ones sit.
3. **Training with surprises.** The controller trained in the Isaac Lab simulator. Each episode, ball weight (45–100 g) and friction were randomized. Two new tricks were added. One limits how fast joints may change, so the policy cannot rely on jerky moves. The other, called "Stuck-At Taxels," freezes up to six touch sensors at a fixed value, so the policy cannot depend on any one sensor.
4. **Calibration and deployment.** Real sensor readings were converted to on/off with tuned thresholds. The policy then ran on the real hand with no extra tuning.

## Results
Each setup got 10 real trials.
- The full method averaged 34.75 full rotations before a drop, versus 0.50 for the version without the sensor-freezing trick. That trick was the key ingredient.
- It spun at about 0.36 rotations per second. Each trial lasted 94.8 seconds on average before a drop.
- Switching off touch at test time cut rotations to 5.0, about 7× fewer. A controller trained with joint sense only reached 4.4.
- Simply replaying a recorded motion without feedback reached 1.7.
- One separate run completed 112.5 full rotations in 310 seconds.
- Prior camera-based work managed roughly 3 rotations in 10 seconds. The authors call their result the strongest hardware Baoding result reported, by count and speed.

## Why it matters
Touch-only control could make robot hands work in the dark, inside bags, or when fingers block the view. The sensor-freezing trick is a cheap, general way to make policies robust to faulty or miscalibrated sensors. It could apply to many other tactile robots.

## Caveats
Results vary a lot: rotations per trial ranged from 2 to 74. Tests used one ball pair, one hand, and one tilt angle. Sensor thresholds and speed limits were hand-tuned for this specific hand. The joint-sense-only policy was trained separately, so it is not a perfect apples-to-apples comparison. Touch is only on/off, which throws away pressure detail.

## Key terms
- **Proprioception**: a robot's sense of its own joint positions and speeds.
- **Taxel**: a single touch-sensing spot, like a pixel for touch.
- **Domain randomization**: varying simulator settings during training so the policy copes with real-world differences.
- **Sim-to-real**: training in simulation, then running on a physical robot.
- **Zero-shot deployment**: running on hardware without any further training there.

papers.title: RL-ARC: Calibrating Large Reasoning Models via Reasoning-guided Uncertainty
papers.tldr: A reinforcement learning reward that checks a model's confidence in both its reasoning and its answer makes reasoning models' stated confidence far more honest, with little loss in accuracy.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
RL-ARC trains reasoning AI models to say how sure they are in a way that actually matches how often they are right, by checking confidence in the reasoning as well as in the final answer.

## Background you need
Large reasoning models write out step-by-step thinking before answering. Many are improved with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR): the model gets a point when its final answer checks out, for example a correct math result. Calibration means that when a model says "80% sure," it is right about 80% of the time. The Brier score measures this gap: lower is better.

## The problem
RLVR only rewards correct answers. It never punishes a model for being confidently wrong, so models drift toward overconfidence. That is risky in places like healthcare or finance, where a user trusts a confident answer. Earlier fixes reward good confidence on the answer itself. They still become overconfident on unfamiliar question types and can cost some accuracy.

## The idea
Picture a student who must write two numbers on every exam answer: how sound their working is, and how sure they are of the final result. A good teacher rewards a confident answer only if the working also looks solid. The teacher also docks marks for confident working that leads to a wrong answer. RL-ARC applies that teacher's logic during training.

## How it works
1. **Ask for two confidences.** The model states a reasoning confidence (is my logic sound?) and an answer confidence (is my answer right?) as part of its output.
2. **Base reward.** It still earns a point for a correct answer, as in normal RLVR.
3. **Calibration penalty.** A Brier-style penalty lowers the reward when answer confidence does not match whether the answer was right.
4. **Reasoning check.** If the answer is right, the model is nudged to keep its answer confidence close to its reasoning confidence. If the answer is wrong, high reasoning confidence is penalized.
5. **Training.** The authors use GRPO, a common RL method, on the Big-Math dataset. They test Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B and a distilled Llama-8B.

## Results
Tests covered familiar math (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME) and unfamiliar tasks, such as science questions (GPQA) and trivia (TriviaQA). ECE is the average gap between stated confidence and real accuracy, so lower is better.
- On Qwen2.5-7B math, RL-ARC kept accuracy at 56.53%, close to plain RLVR's 56.86%. Its ECE fell to 0.18, from 0.40 for RLVR and 0.22 for RLCR, the strongest earlier method.
- On unfamiliar tasks, RL-ARC's ECE was 0.16, versus 0.20 for RLCR and 0.50 for RLVR. Accuracy stayed similar (47.27% vs 47.58% for RLVR).
- On Qwen3-8B math, it scored 66.10% accuracy, and its AUROC (how well confidence separates right from wrong) rose to 0.83 from RLCR's 0.76.
- An ablation showed both pieces help. The overconfidence penalty mainly improves calibration, and the reasoning check mainly helps accuracy.

## Why it matters
A model whose "I'm 90% sure" means something lets products route low-confidence answers to a human or a second check. That is useful for assistants in medicine, law or finance. RL-ARC adds this almost for free on top of standard RL training, with little accuracy loss.

## Caveats
Only two training data types (math and multi-step questions) and one RL algorithm were tested. Most experiments use Qwen models, and multimodal models were not studied. The Llama model still lost some accuracy on unfamiliar tasks. Judging whether reasoning was correct relied on another AI acting as a grader, which can make mistakes.

## Key terms
- **RLVR**: reinforcement learning where reward comes from automatically checkable answers.
- **Calibration**: how well stated confidence matches actual accuracy.
- **Brier score**: the squared gap between confidence and the actual right-or-wrong outcome, where lower is better.
- **ECE (expected calibration error)**: the average mismatch between confidence and accuracy across confidence levels.
- **Out-of-distribution**: test questions unlike anything seen in training.

papers.title: How RL Reshapes LLM Reasoning: Transferability, Coverage, and Scaling Laws
papers.tldr: Reinforcement learning mostly reshuffles which reasoning strategies a language model favors, which explains why it can help some tasks, hurt others, and shrink the range of problems the model can solve.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper studies what reinforcement learning really does to a language model's reasoning, and finds it mostly reshuffles which strategies the model prefers rather than teaching it new ones.

## Background you need
After pre-training, many language models are tuned with reinforcement learning (RL): they try problems and get rewarded for correct answers. Pass@1 is the chance the first attempt is right. Pass@N is the chance that at least one of N attempts is right, which measures "coverage," the range of problems the model can ever solve. A scaling law is a formula that predicts performance from how much computing power you spend.

## The problem
Reports about RL conflict. Training on math sometimes helps coding and sometimes hurts it. RL often raises Pass@1 while lowering Pass@1024 compared with the original model. Nobody had a clear account of why. Labs deciding how much compute to spend on RL also need to know whether gains will keep coming.

## The idea
Think of the model as a chef with a recipe box. RL does not hand the chef new recipes. It moves some cards to the front and buries others. Dishes needing the favored recipes improve. Dishes needing buried recipes get worse, or are rarely attempted. The authors separate "choose a strategy" from "carry it out" to study this reshuffling.

## How it works
1. **Train real models.** They train Qwen3-14B-Base and Gemma-3-12B-IT with GRPO, a common RL method, on 48,000 math problems. One Qwen variant also gets 5,000 coding problems. For comparison, they also do supervised fine-tuning (SFT), meaning copying worked examples, on 40,000 math solutions.
2. **Measure transfer and coverage.** They test math, coding, knowledge, planning and general tasks. They compare Pass@1 and Pass@1024 against the starting model.
3. **Count strategies.** For 240 questions, they sample 16 answers per model. Another AI labels the strategy each answer uses, so they can count distinct "routes."
4. **Build a simple theory.** A two-stage toy model, one part picking a strategy and one part executing it, lets them prove how RL shifts strategy preferences.
5. **Fit scaling laws.** They fit two curve shapes, log-sigmoid and log-linear, to results over 200 training steps. Then they check predictions out to roughly double the compute.

## Results
- Math scores improved consistently. Effects elsewhere diverged: trained on the same data, Qwen and Gemma moved in opposite directions on many other tasks.
- The most common pattern was higher Pass@1 but lower Pass@1024. For example, Qwen narrowed its coverage on the AIME 2024 math contest.
- Coverage can grow when success is rare. On the BoxNet planning task, Qwen's Pass@1 rose from 3.8% to 9.9%, and its Pass@1024 from 34.0% to 51.0%.
- The average number of distinct strategies per question fell from 3.24 to 2.66. Still, 12.7% of RL answers used a strategy absent from the base model's 16 samples.
- Both curve shapes fit training data very closely and predicted math well at double compute. Coding and planning were less predictable, and the log-linear curve tended to over-predict.

## Why it matters
It explains why RL can raise headline scores while quietly shrinking what a model can do. Teams training reasoning models can use this to choose data mixes. It also suggests watching Pass@N, not just Pass@1, and using the scaling fits to budget compute.

## Caveats
The theory uses a heavily simplified model with idealized assumptions. Experiments cover only two model families and a few data mixes. Strategy labels come from another AI, on 240 questions. Scaling predictions are shakier outside math. Some detailed numbers sit in tables not reviewed here.

## Key terms
- **Pass@N**: the chance at least one of N tries is correct; a measure of coverage.
- **GRPO**: a popular RL method that compares several answers to the same question to decide which to reinforce.
- **SFT (supervised fine-tuning)**: training a model to copy example solutions.
- **Scaling law**: a formula predicting performance from compute spent.
- **Forgetting**: losing skills on other tasks after training on one.
